paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for convex optimization problems whose objectives combine different kinds of terms, including nonsmooth ones. It uses conditional gradient methods, which organize optimization around linear subproblems. The aim is to accommodate a broad collection of problems within a single framework while retaining a provable convergence rate.

The approach combines smoothing with homotopy: it makes difficult terms smoother and changes the approximation as optimization proceeds. The authors prove that their framework achieves an optimal convergence rate. They also show that this rate survives when the linear subproblems are solved approximately, under the additive or multiplicative error formulations they analyze. This makes approximate subproblem solutions part of the theoretical framework.

A further contribution is a convergence characterization when the nonsmooth term is an indicator function, allowing constraints to enter the formulation. Applications include nonsmooth minimization, semidefinite programming, and linear inclusion constraints over a compact domain. Numerical results support the framework’s benefits alongside its theoretical guarantees.
icml-2018-a-conditional-gradient-framewo.tldr: A conditional gradient framework combines smoothing and homotopy to achieve optimal convergence rates, including with approximate linear subproblem solutions.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix leads to nonconvex optimization problems, where a central concern is whether local minima can be worse than the global optimum. This paper proposes a framework for examining that question through primal-dual analysis, connecting the original recovery problem with its dual description.

The analysis assumes restricted strong convexity and smoothness, conditions the authors say can be verified for a broad family of loss functions. It also handles incoherence constraints directly through duality. These assumptions and constraints are part of the mathematical setting in which the authors establish their results, rather than a claim about every nonconvex matrix recovery problem.

The framework is applied to matrix completion and one-bit matrix completion, establishing the absence of spurious local minima in the analyzed settings. It improves the sample complexity needed to characterize global optimality for matrix completion and resolves a previously open question for one-bit completion. Numerical experiments further show successful recovery of global optima by a primal-dual algorithm across several low-rank problems.
icml-2018-a-primal-dual-analysis-of-glob.tldr: A primal-dual framework establishes global optimality properties for low-rank recovery under restricted convexity and smoothness conditions.

paragraphs: Learning a latent representation is useful when it supports both generating data and changing meaningful properties of the generated output. This paper addresses that goal for discrete structures, particularly text sequences, where applying approaches developed for continuous data has been more challenging.

The proposed adversarially regularized autoencoder extends the Wasserstein Autoencoder framework to discrete sequences. That framework describes adversarial autoencoders through an optimal transport formulation. The authors also investigate learned priors aimed at making the representation controllable. Together, these choices connect how the model organizes its latent space with the kinds of outputs it can produce.

The resulting model generates fluent text and supports latent-space manipulations that induce changes in the output. The authors further train the representation for unaligned textual style transfer, enabling style changes without aligned source-and-target text examples. They report improvements in both automatic measures and human evaluation. These findings support the representation’s usefulness for controlled text generation, beyond producing text alone.
icml-2018-adversarially-regularized-auto.tldr: An adversarially regularized autoencoder learns controllable text representations that support fluent generation and unaligned style transfer.

paragraphs: Clustering methods such as K-means can be unstable because optimization can become trapped in local minima. Convex clustering offers a different formulation: the sum-of-norms model is a convex relaxation of hierarchical clustering. However, solving this model becomes computationally challenging as the problem grows, even with existing optimization algorithms.

The paper proposes an augmented Lagrangian method built around a semismooth Newton approach for large-scale convex clustering. Its contribution concerns how to solve the clustering optimization problem efficiently. The motivation is that a useful convex formulation also needs a practical solver if it is to handle large datasets.

Experiments on simulated and real data show that the proposed algorithm is efficient and robust on large problems. The reported numerical comparisons also favor it over existing first-order methods in performance and scalability. These findings support the method as a computational improvement for convex clustering; the abstract’s central result is about solving the model effectively, rather than a new criterion for judging the resulting clusters.
icml-2018-an-efficient-semismooth-newton.tldr: A semismooth Newton augmented Lagrangian solver makes large-scale convex clustering more efficient in reported experiments.

paragraphs: An agent may encounter tasks after training that it has never practiced directly. This paper studies how learning the effects of actions on important environmental properties can support such tasks. Its setup provides user-defined attributes describing the features of interest, so goals can be expressed in terms of those attributes.

The method learns a policy for moving between nearby attribute configurations and records possible transitions in a graph. At test time, it infers the attributes of the current state and searches the graph for a route to the target configuration. This route supplies a high-level plan, while the learned policy carries out its individual transitions.

The key idea is to reuse short, learned behaviors as components of longer plans. Experiments in block stacking, grid-world games, and StarCraft show generalization to longer and more complex tasks through this composition. The stated setup requires that a test-time task be expressible as a target set of attributes, tying the planning capability to the properties supplied for the environment.
icml-2018-composable-planning-with-attri.tldr: An agent plans through a graph of user-defined attributes, composing learned local policies to solve longer tasks at test time.

paragraphs: Time series can combine abrupt events with smoother evolution. A burst of activity in a social network, for example, may be followed by gradual diffusion. The paper argues that a simple dynamic model struggles with this mixture, while an off-the-shelf deep network is less naturally suited to discovering sparse, discrete changes.

The proposed model combines Bayesian nonparametric methods with a deep neural network. The Bayesian component models change-point behavior over time, using probabilistic assumptions to represent irregular events. The neural component handles nonlinear dynamics in latent space. This division gives the model separate ways to describe abrupt changes and the evolving patterns surrounding them.

The authors also propose a linear version without the deep component and use it as a comparison. Evaluations on stock prices and Twitter trends report improved performance and interpretable tracking results. The findings support combining structured probabilistic modeling with learned nonlinear dynamics when the data contain both irregular events and smoother temporal behavior.
icml-2018-deep-bayesian-nonparametric-tr.tldr: A combined Bayesian and deep learning model tracks time series by separating change-point behavior from nonlinear latent dynamics.

paragraphs: Video and audio contain both properties that persist through a sequence and properties that change over time. This paper introduces a variational autoencoder that represents these two kinds of information separately. Its latent representation contains a static part for content and a dynamic part for temporal behavior.

The separation is approximate, giving partial control over generation by conditioning on one set of features or the other. In experiments with generated cartoon clips and voice recordings, the authors demonstrate content swapping between sequences. The reported examples include converting voices between male and female speakers and separately changing video shapes and dynamics.

The paper also examines how latent temporal states should be modeled. Its experiments support the hypothesis that stochastic recurrent networks compress and generate long sequences more efficiently than deterministic ones. The authors identify possible relevance to video compression. Together, these results connect a structured latent representation with controllable generation and provide empirical support for stochastic models of long sequences.
icml-2018-disentangled-sequential-autoen.tldr: A sequential variational autoencoder approximately separates persistent content from changing dynamics, enabling partial control and content swapping.

paragraphs: Online learning in a changing environment needs ways to measure whether a learner keeps adapting. Adaptive regret and dynamic regret approach this concern from different directions. This paper connects them by showing how dynamic regret can be expressed using adaptive regret together with functional variation, a measure of how the learning problem changes.

That connection makes strongly adaptive algorithms useful for controlling dynamic regret directly. The authors develop a series of such algorithms for convex, exponentially concave, and strongly convex functions. The result gives a common route to dynamic regret guarantees across these different classes, rather than treating adaptation and changing objectives as separate topics.

A practical feature is that the algorithms do not require advance knowledge of functional variation. They therefore avoid needing the amount of environmental change as an input. The authors also identify their use of exponential concavity to bound dynamic regret as a first, to their knowledge. Overall, the contribution is a theoretical bridge that yields algorithms with small dynamic regret.
icml-2018-dynamic-regret-of-strongly-ada.tldr: A connection between adaptive and dynamic regret yields algorithms that handle changing objectives without knowing their variation in advance.

paragraphs: Inductive matrix completion seeks to recover a low-rank matrix using both observed information and known features supplied as prior information. The central question here is whether those features can reduce both the amount of data needed and the computational effort required for recovery. The paper studies a rank-r matrix with ambient dimension d and n supplied features.

The authors introduce and analyze a gradient-based nonconvex optimization algorithm. They establish linear convergence to the underlying matrix, meaning that recovery error decreases at a geometric rate in their analysis. Its sample complexity depends linearly on the number of features and logarithmically on the ambient dimension.

These two properties address a tradeoff in earlier work: according to the authors, previous algorithms had either quadratic feature dependence in sample complexity or sublinear computational convergence. The proposed method combines improved feature dependence with fast convergence. Experiments on synthetic and real data further demonstrate its effectiveness, complementing the theoretical analysis of data requirements and optimization speed.
icml-2018-fast-and-sample-efficient-indu.tldr: A nonconvex gradient method combines linear convergence for inductive matrix completion with sample complexity linear in the number of supplied features.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning by agents connected through a communication network that may be sparse and may change over time. Each agent has its own reward function, potentially corresponding to a different task, and that reward function is known only to that agent. Decisions depend on local observations and messages from neighboring agents.

Despite these local information boundaries, the collective objective is to maximize the average return across the network. The authors propose two fully decentralized actor-critic algorithms for this purpose. Their approach is designed for online use in large-scale multi-agent problems, allowing agents to learn through local computation and communication.

The paper provides convergence guarantees when value functions are represented using linear function approximation. That qualification is central to the stated theory. The authors describe the work as apparently the first theoretical study of fully decentralized, networked multi-agent reinforcement learning with function approximation. Its contribution is to connect a shared learning objective with decentralized decisions and a mathematically analyzed approximation setting.
icml-2018-fully-decentralized-multi-agen.tldr: Two decentralized actor-critic algorithms optimize network-wide average return, with convergence guarantees for linear value-function approximation.

paragraphs: GAIN adapts adversarial learning to filling missing entries in data. Its generator receives the observed components of a data vector and uses them to generate replacements for the missing components. The output is a completed vector that combines real observations with generated values.

The discriminator examines that vector and predicts which individual components were originally observed and which were filled in. The method also gives the discriminator a hint containing partial information about the original missingness pattern. This information focuses the discriminator’s attention on the quality of particular imputations. The hint is central to the authors’ argument that the generator learns the true data distribution.

This setup makes imputation depend on the available information within each sample, while adversarial feedback evaluates the generated components. Across the datasets tested, the authors report that GAIN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods. The findings support the proposed combination of component-level discrimination and missingness hints as an effective way to learn data completion.
icml-2018-gain-missing-data-imputation-u.tldr: GAIN fills missing data through adversarial learning, using partial missingness hints to guide component-level discrimination.

paragraphs: Generating graphs is difficult because graphs have nonunique representations, many possible connections, and dependencies between edges that can extend across the structure. GraphRNN addresses this by learning from a representative collection of graphs. The authors present it as a model capable of approximating any graph distribution with minimal structural assumptions.

GraphRNN generates a graph through a sequence of node and edge additions. Each step depends on the structure already produced, allowing earlier choices to inform later connections. This autoregressive formulation turns generation into a series of conditional decisions while retaining information about the growing graph.

The paper also introduces a benchmark suite and evaluation measures based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy to compare sets of graphs. In the reported experiments, GraphRNN significantly outperforms all included baselines and generates diverse graphs matching the target collection’s structural characteristics. It also scales to graphs fifty times larger than previous deep models. These results address both the quality of generated structures and the size of graphs the approach can handle.
icml-2018-graphrnn-generating-realistic-.tldr: GraphRNN generates graphs through conditional node and edge additions, producing diverse structures and scaling beyond earlier deep models in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Distributed ADMM algorithms let nodes compute on local data and repeatedly exchange outputs with neighbors. Those exchanges can reveal private information. The paper highlights a difficulty with earlier privacy analysis: bounding the loss for one node in one iteration does not readily explain the privacy and utility tradeoff across the entire network and iterative process.

The authors modify ADMM so that each node independently chooses its penalty parameter at every iteration. They also separate that parameter from the step size used for dual updates. On top of this modification, they introduce a perturbation method whose added term is correlated with the penalty parameters.

The proposed construction is shown to improve utility and privacy simultaneously. The paper also derives a convergence condition for the modified algorithm and a lower bound on its convergence rate. These results connect the design of privacy-preserving perturbations with the underlying optimization procedure, treating parameter choice as part of how distributed learning balances useful computation and privacy.
icml-2018-improving-the-privacy-and-accu.tldr: An ADMM modification links privacy perturbations to locally chosen penalty parameters, improving privacy and utility together.

paragraphs: Topic models are useful for understanding text when their discovered themes are interpretable as well as accurate. This paper proposes a model that represents structure at two levels: relationships between topics and finer distinctions within each topic. Word embeddings inform both kinds of structure.

Between topics, the model learns a hierarchy that organizes their relationships. Within a topic, it learns subtopics describing more specific thematic aspects. Its deep structure brings these views together, giving a way to understand both how themes relate across a collection and how an individual theme breaks into finer parts.

The authors report state-of-the-art results in their experiments on perplexity, document classification, and topic quality. They also find the resulting topics more interpretable because the hierarchy and subtopics expose organization that would otherwise remain hidden inside broader themes. The contribution therefore combines improved reported modeling performance with a more structured account of what the model discovers in text.
icml-2018-inter-and-intra-topic-structur.tldr: A topic model uses word embeddings to learn topic hierarchies and finer subtopics, improving reported performance and interpretability.

paragraphs: Sparse inverse covariance estimation is often performed with graphical lasso, but its computational cost can become prohibitive at large scale. This paper builds on results connecting that estimator to a different route: soft-threshold the sample covariance matrix, then solve a maximum determinant matrix completion problem. The earlier connection holds under mild assumptions.

The authors extend this connection and introduce a Newton-CG algorithm for the resulting completion problem. Their efficiency guarantee assumes that the thresholded covariance matrix is sparse and also has a sparse Cholesky factorization. Under that structure, the algorithm reaches accuracy epsilon in O(n log(1/epsilon)) time using O(n) memory.

The practical results demonstrate the scale this approach can reach. The authors solve associated completion problems with up to 200,000 variables to seven to nine digits of accuracy in under an hour on a standard laptop running MATLAB. The significance is a computational route to large problems whose efficiency is explicitly tied to the sparsity structure used by the algorithm.
icml-2018-large-scale-sparse-inverse-cov.tldr: A thresholding and matrix-completion approach enables efficient sparse inverse covariance estimation under specified sparsity assumptions.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks can struggle to learn relationships across long sequences because training gradients shrink or grow excessively before reaching earlier steps. The Fourier Recurrent Unit addresses this by changing how information from hidden states is summarized over time. It uses Fourier basis functions to represent that temporal information.

The architecture combines this summary with a residual learning structure. Because trigonometric functions have support across time, the authors explain that gradients can reach earlier layers more readily. They establish upper and lower gradient bounds that do not depend on the temporal dimension, directly addressing the role of sequence length in gradient stability.

The paper also analyzes the expressive strength of sparse Fourier bases, linking that property to the architecture’s ability to represent temporal patterns. Experiments show that the proposed network outperforms other recurrent architectures on many tasks while using fewer parameters. The contribution brings together a theoretical argument for stable gradient propagation, an expressivity analysis, and empirical evidence of effective sequence learning.
icml-2018-learning-long-term-dependencie.tldr: Fourier Recurrent Units summarize hidden states with Fourier functions, yielding sequence-length-independent gradient bounds and strong reported performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks aim to combine flexible prediction with uncertainty estimates, but approximating their posterior distributions can be costly. Simple approximation families are cheaper, while richer ones often require complicated inference. This paper identifies a connection that turns familiar optimization methods into tools for variational Bayesian learning.

The authors show that natural gradient ascent with adaptive noise on the weights implicitly fits a variational posterior by maximizing the evidence lower bound. Noisy natural gradient, Adam, and K-FAC support full-covariance, fully factorized, and matrix-variate Gaussian posteriors, respectively. This provides several choices of posterior structure and makes training modern-sized convolutional networks feasible.

On standard regression benchmarks, noisy K-FAC produces better predictions and predictive variances closer to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo than existing methods. The paper also reports that improved uncertainty estimates support more efficient exploration in active learning and intrinsic motivation for reinforcement learning. The practical value of the connection therefore extends from scalable inference to decisions that depend on uncertainty.
icml-2018-noisy-natural-gradient-as-vari.tldr: Adaptive weight noise turns natural-gradient-based optimization into variational inference, enabling scalable Bayesian neural networks with improved reported uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Policy optimization usually adjusts a policy’s parameters to increase expected reward or a related objective. This paper asks how such updates relate mathematically to optimizing distributions. It moves the problem into a space of probability measures and interprets policy improvement through Wasserstein gradient flows.

Under specified circumstances, the distribution-level formulation becomes convex. This is a conditional property of the formulation. To turn the perspective into usable algorithms, the authors numerically solve discrete versions of the corresponding gradient flows. They define flows both over distributions of parameters and over distributions of policies, producing indirect-policy and direct-policy learning frameworks.

The approach applies to several reinforcement learning settings and connects with a number of existing policy optimization algorithms. Extensive experiments support its effectiveness, often showing better performance than related methods. Its contribution is therefore both conceptual and computational: it clarifies a distribution-based interpretation of policy optimization and uses that interpretation to construct algorithms evaluated on reinforcement learning tasks.
icml-2018-policy-optimization-as-wassers.tldr: Policy optimization is recast as Wasserstein gradient flows over distributions, yielding conditional convexity and practical reinforcement learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Metric-based individual fairness asks that people considered similar by a task-specific metric receive similar treatment. Requiring this for every pair creates a learning difficulty: fairness on training examples does not automatically generalize to the population. The paper shows that this issue can make even simple fair-learning tasks computationally intractable.

The authors relax the requirement to randomly sampled pairs from the population. Similar individuals should receive similar treatment except with a small probability of error. They formalize learning under this requirement as Probably Approximately Correct and Fair learning, combining approximate metric fairness with the goal of best-possible accuracy.

The central result is that this approximate fairness notion does generalize. The authors use that guarantee to construct polynomial-time learning algorithms for linear and logistic predictors. The relaxation matters because it turns a population-wide fairness goal into one that can be learned efficiently for these predictor classes, while explicitly allowing a small probability of fairness violations.
icml-2018-probably-approximately-metric-.tldr: Allowing a small probability of metric-fairness violations enables generalization guarantees and efficient fair learning for linear and logistic predictors.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits and Markov decision processes are two common ways to model learning through decisions under uncertainty. This paper asks whether an algorithm designed for the more general MDP setting can automatically enjoy stronger performance guarantees when the actual problem has the simpler structure of a contextual bandit.

The authors analyze a very small modification of a recently proposed MDP reinforcement learning algorithm. When deployed on a tabular contextual bandit problem, it matches the best possible regret bound in the dominant term: approximately the square root of SAT, up to logarithmic factors. The agent does not need to be told that it is operating in the bandit setting.

The result shows that a general-purpose reinforcement learning procedure can adapt to this particular simpler structure without user intervention or a setting-specific algorithm change at deployment. Its precision matters: the optimality statement concerns the dominant regret term for tabular contextual bandits. This gives a concrete example of problem-dependent guarantees within a broader reinforcement learning framework.
icml-2018-problem-dependent-reinforcemen.tldr: A small variant of an MDP learning algorithm achieves the optimal dominant regret term on tabular contextual bandits without knowing the setting.

paragraphs: A target prediction task may have too little data to train a complex model well, even when related datasets exist elsewhere. Those external datasets come from different sources, so making them useful for the target setting is itself a learning problem. RadialGAN addresses this situation by learning translations between datasets.

The method uses multiple generative adversarial network architectures to map data from one dataset to another. These translations allow information from related sources to enlarge the target dataset effectively. The objective is to improve the predictive model for that specific target domain by making additional data useful in its setting.

On a collection of real-world medical datasets, the authors report better target-domain prediction than training with the target dataset alone. They also report improvements over several comparison methods. These results support learned dataset translation as a way to benefit from multiple related sources when target data are scarce, with the demonstrated gains belonging to the medical datasets evaluated.
icml-2018-radialgan-leveraging-multiple-.tldr: RadialGAN learns translations among related datasets to expand target-domain training data and improve prediction in reported medical-data experiments.

paragraphs: Submodular function minimization is a discrete optimization problem with applications in machine learning and computer vision, but large instances remain expensive. This paper brings screening techniques from sparse learning into that setting. The aim is to identify decisions that can be settled before the full optimization process finishes.

The method builds on relationships between submodular minimization and associated convex proximal problems, together with estimates of those problems’ primal optima. It uses this analysis to identify elements guaranteed to belong to the final optimal solution and elements guaranteed to be absent. Those guarantees are what make the screening safe.

Once an element’s status is established, the algorithm can fix it as included or remove it from further consideration. This can shrink the remaining problem substantially without sacrificing accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show significant speedups. The contribution is therefore a way to reduce computational work by proving some decisions early, while preserving the optimization result.
icml-2018-safe-element-screening-for-sub.tldr: Safe screening accelerates submodular minimization by fixing guaranteed inclusion and exclusion decisions without sacrificing solution accuracy.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior using a chosen family of distributions. This paper broadens that family by treating its parameters as draws from another, more flexible distribution. The resulting mixture can represent richer posterior shapes, including implicit distributions without an analytic density function.

The mixing distribution need not have an explicit density, but it must support independent sampling through reparameterization. This flexibility creates an optimization challenge because the evidence lower bound can become difficult to work with directly. The authors address it by constructing lower and upper bounds on that objective and deriving an asymptotically exact surrogate suitable for stochastic gradient ascent.

The method therefore combines a more expressive approximation family with a way to optimize it. Across a variety of Bayesian inference tasks, the authors report posterior inference accuracy close to that of MCMC. This empirical finding supports the usefulness of the expanded family and optimization method together, while the surrogate’s exactness is specifically an asymptotic result.
icml-2018-semi-implicit-variational-infe.tldr: Semi-implicit variational inference combines flexible parameter mixtures with an optimizable surrogate objective, closely matching MCMC accuracy in reported tasks.

paragraphs: Training recurrent networks on long-range dependencies is difficult when gradients vanish or explode. Spectral-RNN addresses this by representing the recurrent transition matrix through its singular value decomposition. This exposes the singular values directly so that the method can track and control them during training.

The orthogonal matrices in the decomposition are represented efficiently using Householder reflectors. Explicit singular-value control addresses exploding gradients, while the authors observe that vanishing gradients are also reduced substantially in experiments. They prove that the parameterization preserves expressive power and explain how it could make optimization easier. Because it applies to rectangular weight matrices, it can also extend to other deep networks.

Experiments report faster convergence and good generalization, especially for learning long-range dependencies. Evaluations include addition and copy tasks, MNIST, and Penn Tree Bank. The paper thus combines an efficient matrix representation with direct control over properties relevant to gradient propagation, while distinguishing its theoretical expressivity result from its empirical findings about vanishing gradients.
icml-2018-stabilizing-gradients-for-deep.tldr: Spectral-RNN efficiently controls singular values to stabilize training gradients while preserving expressive power.

paragraphs: This paper connects feedforward ReLU neural networks with tropical geometry, providing a geometric language for studying the functions these networks represent. Its central result identifies the family of such networks with the family of tropical rational maps. That correspondence lets questions about network structure be expressed through geometric objects.

For networks with one hidden layer, the authors give a characterization using zonotopes, which become building blocks for deeper networks. They also relate decision boundaries to tropical hypersurfaces. A further result connects the network’s linear regions with vertices of polytopes associated with tropical rational functions, translating the subdivision of its input space into a geometric relationship.

These connections make the representation of shallow and deep networks accessible through the same mathematical framework. One insight is an exponential expressivity advantage for deeper networks over shallow ones. The contribution concerns what the networks can represent and how that capacity is organized geometrically; its stated findings are mathematical connections and expressivity results.
icml-2018-tropical-geometry-of-deep-neur.tldr: Tropical geometry characterizes ReLU networks through geometric objects and reveals an exponential expressivity advantage of depth.
